questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Total body calcium (1000–1300 g) resides in bones to the extent of:
questions.exp: 99.3% bones, 0.6% soft tissue, 0.1% ECF. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Match the soft-tissue calcium fractions — 1) Free (ionized)  2) Bound to albumin  3) Bound to other proteins … A) 40%  B) 12%  C) 48%
questions.exp: Soft-tissue calcium: 48% free ionized, 40% albumin-bound, 12% other proteins. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: The normal corrected calcium range is:
questions.exp: Normal corrected Ca2+ 8.6–10.3 mg/dL. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Corrected Ca2+ = Total Ca2+ + ___.
questions.exp: Corrected Ca = Total Ca + 0.8 (4 − albumin level). (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Corrected calcium defines hypocalcaemia below and hypercalcaemia above:
questions.exp: <8.4 mg/dL hypocalcaemia; >10.5 mg/dL hypercalcaemia. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Free ionized calcium functions include sensitizing CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity and:
questions.exp: Functions: sensitize CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity, bone mineralization. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: ‘In acidosis, H+ competes with calcium for albumin, raising the free Ca2+.’
questions.exp: ↑ H+ (acidosis) → ↑ free Ca2+; ↓ pH by 0.1 unit → ↑ Ca2+ by 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: A fall in pH by 0.1 unit raises ionized calcium by:
questions.exp: ↓ pH 0.1 unit → ↑ Ca2+ 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Plasma calcium equals:
opts: Free Ca2+ plus Ca2+ complexed to anions
questions.exp: Plasma Ca = free Ca2+ + Ca2+ complexed to anions. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Calcium absorption occurs in the proximal small intestine with the order:
questions.exp: Site: proximal small intestine (jejunum > duodenum); ~20% net absorption (~200 mg), enhanced by acid. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Match absorption route — 1) 95% active transcellular  2) 5% passive paracellular … A) Independent of calcitriol  B) Tightly controlled by calcitriol
questions.exp: 95% active transcellular (calcitriol-controlled); 5% passive paracellular (independent). (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Calcitriol drives transcellular calcium absorption by:
opts: Binding nuclear receptors → releasing calbindin → activating TRPV5/6; exit via Ca2+ ATPase
questions.exp: Calcitriol binds nuclear receptors, releases calbindin, activates TRPV5/6; calcium exits via Ca2+ ATPase. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: Free ionized calcium functions listed are sensitizing CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity and bone mineralization. Pick the ODD ONE OUT:
questions.exp: Ionized Ca sensitizes CaSR and drives contractility, neuromuscular activity and mineralization — suppression is the odd one. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Calcium distribution, corrected calcium and absorption · p874
questions.q: A patient's ABG shows pH 7.25. The expected effect on serum calcium is:
opts: Acidosis raises free ionized Ca2+ as H+ competes with Ca2+ for albumin
Acidosis lowers free ionized Ca2+ by albumin binding
No change in the ionized fraction
questions.exp: H+ competes for albumin: acidosis increases free Ca; ↓pH 0.1 → ↑Ca 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: Daily urinary calcium loss is approximately:
questions.exp: ~200 mg lost in urine; 4 mg/kg/24 hours; >4 mg/kg/day = hypercalciuria. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: Match the ‘4/7/11’ stone thresholds — 1) >4 mg/kg/24 hr  2) >7 mg/24 hr  3) <11 mg/kg/24 hr … A) Hyperuricosuria (2nd m/c)  B) Hypocitraturia  C) Hypercalciuria (m/c)
questions.exp: m/c causes of stones: hypercalciuria >4 mg/kg/24 hr (m/c), hyperuricosuria >7 mg/24 hr (2nd m/c), hypocitraturia <11 mg/kg/24 hr. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: Milk-alkali syndrome begins with excess calcium consumption above:
questions.exp: Excess Ca2+ consumption >4 g/day → ↑ paracellular Ca2+ entry. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: In milk-alkali syndrome, hypercalcaemia activates CaSR which then:
opts: Reduces Ca2+ absorption and ADH → volume depletion → RAAS → metabolic alkalosis
questions.exp: Hypercalcaemia (+) CaSR (−) → ↓ Ca2+ absorption and ↓ ADH → volume depletion → RAAS → metabolic alkalosis; also hypercalciuria → stones. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: Match renal calcium handling — 1) PCT  2) TAL  3) DCT … A) 25%, paracellular, PTH-dependent  B) 10%, active transport, most dependent  C) 65%, paracellular, PTH-independent
questions.exp: PCT 65% paracellular independent; TAL 25% paracellular dependent; DCT 10% active transport most dependent. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: A rise in ionized calcium triggers, within SECONDS, the:
opts: Parathyroid CaSR inhibiting PTH release → hypocalcaemia (immediate response)
questions.exp: Within seconds: parathyroid CaSR (−) PTH release → hypocalcaemia (immediate). (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: Within a FEW DAYS, raised ionized calcium acts on the kidney (TAL) CaSR to cause:
questions.exp: Delayed response: kidney (TAL) CaSR (−) Ca2+ reabsorption → hypercalciuria; vice-versa when ionized calcium falls. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Excretion, stone thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal handling · p875
questions.q: In the TAL diagram, the claudins shown regulating paracellular calcium are:
questions.exp: TAL regulation involves CLDN 16/19 and claudin-14, with PTH raising absorption and CaSR raising excretion. (Book p875)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: Match half-lives — 1) PTH  2) Calcitriol  3) 25(OH)D3 … A) 6–8 hours  B) 2–3 weeks  C) 2–4 minutes
questions.exp: PTH 2–4 min; calcitriol 6–8 hours; 25(OH)D3 2–3 weeks (used for blood level estimations). (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: The metabolite used for blood-level estimation of vitamin D (longest half-life) is:
questions.exp: 25(OH)D3 (2–3 weeks) is used for blood level estimations. (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: A GAIN-of-function CaSR mutation causes:
questions.exp: Gain-of-function CaSR → Bartter type V, AD (all other Bartter types AR). (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: ‘Bartter syndrome type V is autosomal dominant, whereas all other Bartter types are autosomal recessive.’
opts: True, but type V is X-linked
questions.exp: Type V AD; all other Bartter types AR. (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: In Bartter type V, excessive CaSR activation causes:
questions.exp: Excessive CaSR activation → ↑↑↑ excretion → hypocalcaemia; all other Bartters show hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: A LOSS-of-function CaSR mutation (seen in children, AD) produces:
questions.exp: Loss-of-function → FHH, autosomal dominant, seen in children. (Book p876)

questions.sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876
questions.q: The FHH pathway is:
opts: Failure of CaSR activation → no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia
questions.exp: Failure of CaSR activation → no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)

units.title: Calcium stores, corrected calcium and intestinal absorption
units.guide: Total 1000–1300 g: 99.3% bone, 0.6% soft tissue (48% ionized, 40% albumin, 12% other), 0.1% ECF. Corrected Ca 8.6–10.3; formula +0.8(4−albumin); <8.4 hypo, >10.5 hyper. Ionized Ca: CaSR sensitisation, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity, bone mineralization; acidosis ↑ free Ca (0.1 pH → 0.1 meq/L). Absorption jejunum > duodenum, 20% net (~200 mg), acid enhances; 95% transcellular calcitriol-controlled (nuclear receptor → calbindin → TRPV5/6 → Ca-ATPase), 5% paracellular independent.

units.title: Urinary thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal calcium handling
units.guide: ~200 mg/day urinary loss; 4 mg/kg/24 h; stones '4/7/11': hypercalciuria >4 (m/c), hyperuricosuria >7 (2nd), hypocitraturia <11. Milk-alkali: >4 g/day intake → paracellular entry → hypercalciuria/stones + hypercalcaemia → CaSR → ↓absorption & ↓ADH → volume depletion → RAAS → metabolic alkalosis. Renal: PCT 65% paracellular independent; TAL 25% dependent; DCT 10% active most dependent. ↑Ionized Ca: seconds → parathyroid CaSR ↓PTH (immediate); days → TAL CaSR ↓reabsorption → hypercalciuria (delayed). TAL CLDN16/19 + claudin-14.

units.title: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders
units.guide: Half-lives PTH 2–4 min, calcitriol 6–8 h, 25(OH)D3 2–3 wks (assay form). Gain-of-function CaSR = Bartter type V (AD; others AR): ↑↑↑ excretion → hypocalcaemia (others hypercalcaemia). Loss-of-function = FHH (children, AD): no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia.
